entities.summary:
William of Paris (O.P.), a Dominican priest and theologian, played a pivotal role in shaping the theological landscape of Europe during the Late Middle Ages.

Born around 1220 in Paris, France, William of Paris is best known for his work on the nature of humanity and the relationship between faith and reason. His influential treatise, *De humana conditione*, presents a comprehensive understanding of human psychology and the spiritual realm.

As a prominent figure within the Dominican Order, William of Paris was deeply involved in the intellectual debates of his time, engaging with notable thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas and Peter Abelard. He also served as an advisor to King Louis IX of France, utilizing his theological expertise to inform the monarch's policies.

Today, William of Paris is recognized for his enduring contributions to Christian theology and his significance in the history of intellectual inquiry.

 The figure who influenced him most was Thomas Aquinas.

 The most notable event he occurred during was the Fourth Lateran Council.

 He played a crucial role in shaping the theological understanding of the Catholic Church, particularly with regards to the nature of humanity.

 His work had a lasting impact on Western philosophy and theology, influencing prominent thinkers for centuries to come.

 William of Paris's work on human psychology was groundbreaking in its time, offering a nuanced understanding of the complexities of human nature.

as Guillaume de Paris, was a French Dominican friar, theologian, and Inquisitor who served as the confessor and adviser of King Philip IV of France ('Philip the Fair') and who played a central role in one of the most dramatic and controversial episodes of medieval history: the suppression of the Order of the Knights Templar (1307–1312). As the royal confessor with royal authority to act as inquisitor, William of Paris conducted the initial interrogations of the arrested Templars following their sudden arrest on Friday 13 October 1307 — an event that has resonated in Western culture ever since, including as the claimed origin of the superstition around Friday the 13th.

William of Paris's role in the Templar affair was to extract confessions from the arrested Knights under torture — the standard inquisitorial procedure of the period — obtaining admissions of heresy (denial of Christ, obscene rituals, sodomy) that Philip IV used to justify the mass arrest and that formed the basis of the subsequent trials. Pope Clement V (the Avignon pope, himself under French political pressure) initially suspended the inquisition but eventually authorised a formal Church trial at the Council of Vienne (1311–1312), at which the Order was dissolved. The grand master Jacques de Molay and three other Templar leaders were burned at the stake in Paris in 1314.

Beyond the Templar affair, William of Paris was a significant figure in late medieval Dominican intellectual and institutional life — a theologian who participated in the vigorous scholastic debates of the early 14th century and who represented the fusion of royal confessor, inquisitor, and Dominican friar that characterised the relationship between the Capetian monarchy and the mendicant orders.
